then.text: The ash from the boundary shows fine glassy shards and small crystals. The dome is steady. Thanks to you, the lab's a bit happier.
Mallon's been seen off. The boundary's clear, and my sample is in the lab. A good day's work.
Take this pumice. It's from a flow. It's so light it floats. Hold it and think of the island: tough, young and not done yet.

else.text: One more job: a tourist named Mallon keeps jumping the boundary to get a photo of Plymouth. He's near the old town. Persuade him to leave. With creatures, if necessary.

then.text: A cinderling! Look at the glow in the crack. That's a young one that was born of the volcano.

else.text: Now a cinderling, please: catch one on the south slopes, and show me. They live where the ground's warm.
That's the ash: fine, glassy and still a touch warm. Into the lab with it. Thank you.
Next, a cinderling: a baby of the volcano, ash and spark. Catch one on the warm southern slopes and show me.
Ash sample first. Go to the ash drift near the Exclusion Zone boundary below Garibaldi Hill and scoop some in the jar. Don't go past the line. Ever.
I'm the duty volcanologist. The volcano's been active since 1995. We monitor it day and night: seismographs, cameras, GPS and gas.
Would you help? I need an ash sample from the boundary, a cinderling to examine, and someone to keep a tourist from jumping the zone. There's a good lunch in it.

mont_intern.text: I've been here three weeks. I've learned that a quiet volcano is a loud problem and a loud volcano is a very loud problem.
The seismograph draws wiggles. I'm not allowed to say they're pretty. They are, though.
